source.title: Predict before you train: Scaling Laws for particle physics foundation models
source.authors: Jan-Lucas Uslu; Benjamin Nachman; Christopher Re

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and line breaks have minor text-extraction corruption, but the results and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies scaling-law measurements and a held-out forecasting test to particle-physics jet models, a new modality and training setting for the claim.
record.gate_note: The study fits a Chinchilla-style loss law, tests its predictions on five later-trained models, derives a compute-optimal allocation, and measures downstream performance. The fit uses 136 model/compute cells as an aggregate; the paper does not report each cell's loss in text. Values for published OmniLearned and other taggers are cited comparisons, not newly measured results, so they are not cataloged as rows. Architecture choices are described but not ablated.
record.test_reason: The study fits a Chinchilla-form joint law to a new modality: jet-classification pretraining with a generic transformer. It then tests forecasts on five later runs at up to 113x the fit compute. It also derives a compute-optimal split and relates pretraining loss to downstream tagging. Its own results bear on V2, V3, V5, V6 and V7 in a non-text setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is largely correct. Add two points. First, the 397M frontier model is reported as consistent with published OmniLearned numbers, except in the top-tagging high-purity tail. Second, the data-favoring allocation is explicitly a hypothesis about low information density per particle token, not a measurement.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the Chinchilla joint model-and-data functional form and a fit-then-forecast evaluation, but applies it to a 210-class jet-classification objective and ParticleViT rather than language-model next-token loss. Compute is counted using occupied particle slots, and the fit points are best-loss runs per model/compute cell.
record.method_sensitivity: The allocation estimate is sensitive to the weakly constrained parameter exponent α; L∞ trades off with β. The authors report that least-squares and robust fit objectives, and subsampling, leave L∞ unresolved over a range while barely changing fit quality. Fine-tuning results use five-run means and best test-trajectory values.
record.problems: The scaling law is validated over a finite compute range and one holdout threshold; the study covers one physics domain and two downstream tasks. The compute-optimal size is extrapolated below the smallest model in the grid and depends on a weakly constrained exponent. Fine-tuning summaries select best test-trajectory values rather than using validation-only selection. The downstream loss/rejection ladder results are presented in plots without numerical values for each checkpoint.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported result omitted. Published OmniLearned and other tagger numbers in Tables III–IV are cited comparisons rather than new measurements by this study, so they are not separate rows.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss is not studied. The jet classification loss is covered under V5.
The aspect ratio is held near 100 throughout. Depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count, and the architecture is not ablated.
Image and video models, a separate repeated-data law, and fine-tuning or transfer power laws are not tested.
The predicted compute-optimal model is not trained. The optimum is not read from IsoFLOP minima.

missing.what: Allowing nonzero L∞ along the degeneracy widens β to at most 0.09; fit quality is nearly unchanged across objectives.
The held-out forecast stays accurate through about 2.8 passes over the corpus while the fit runs are sub-epoch. Unique vs repeated data is not separated.

record.verdict_notes: Rows R1–R6 were relinked from V1 to V5 because V1 names language models. The table rows R12–R51 are single values. Their states are re-graded against the smallest frontier model (S) as the reference. Per-checkpoint ladder values exist only in Fig. 2, with no numbers. The loss is a smoothed training-batch loss, not a separate validation loss. The held-out runs use a different batch size (16384 vs 512) and multiple epochs.

versions.untested_parts: The law is tested on ParticleViT jet classification, not language-model next-token prediction; loss is Gaussian-smoothed training-batch cross-entropy on examples not previously seen in sweep runs, rather than a separately defined held-out validation loss.
Forecasts are tested on five later runs up to 3.4 × 10^20 FLOPs, not on larger scales beyond that range or other model families.

The compute-optimal exponents are inferred from this fitted joint law; the paper does not train the predicted compute-optimal model. The result is for one billion jets and one model family, not a universal allocation trend.
Depth, width, and other architecture choices are not varied independently at a fixed parameter count.
The scaling-law test is for jet classification pretraining. The study does not test image/video models, repeated-data scaling laws as a separate regime, or a power law for fine-tuning and transfer.
Downstream predictability is tested on two tagging benchmarks and one model family. It is not tested on arbitrary physics questions or other domains.

The paper reports fit uncertainty and sensitivity to fit objectives and subsampling, and contrasts its fitted exponents with published language-model exponents. It does not isolate all setup choices, nor test whether curves bend away from a power law beyond the measured range.

rows.subject: ParticleViT model-and-data scaling fit (136 fit points)
rows.size_stated: 136 (compute budget, model size) cells; model sizes vary across the ladder
rows.operation_detail: Fit the Chinchilla-style joint model-and-data loss law to the IsoFLOP sweep; select the lowest-loss run per cell.

conditions.value: OmniLearned jet corpus, approximately 1.06 × 10^9 training jets
ten compute budgets, all below 10^19 FLOPs; largest 3 × 10^18 FLOPs

rows.measure: Fitted joint loss law: L(N,D) = A/N^α + B/D^β + L∞; α = 0.225 (10th–90th percentiles 0.14, 0.29), β = 0.0591 (0.057, 0.063), A = 1.95, B = 2.67, L∞ ≲ 0.2 unresolved. Normalized amplitudes: A/N0^α = 0.057 at N0 = 6.6×10^6; B/D0^β = 0.93 at D0 = 6.0×10^7.
rows.value: The fitted parameters and ranges stated in the measure field.
rows.uncertainty: α and β subsample-refit 10th–90th percentiles; L∞ is unresolved and consistent with 0 to approximately 0.2 under reported fits.
rows.note: The paper says the fitting form is the same as Chinchilla's; it reports a much smaller β than the cited language-model fit. The loss is a training-batch quantity; in sweep runs, examples had not previously been seen.
rows.check: V1 names language-model held-out loss. This is a 210-class jet-classification training-batch loss (unseen examples), so it bears on V5, not V1.

rows.subject: ParticleViT compute-optimal allocation inferred from fitted law
rows.operation_detail: Derive optimal parameter/data allocation as a function of compute from the fitted exponents.

conditions.value: Full corpus of approximately one billion jets
Nominal fit; exponent uncertainty from 100 random 80% subsamples

rows.measure: Nopt ∝ C^a with a = 0.21 (10th–90th-percentile range 0.17–0.30); corresponding Dopt ∝ C^0.79. The fitted optimal size is at or below 10^5 parameters at the full-corpus budget.
rows.baseline: Language-model comparison cited in paper: approximately one parameter per twenty training tokens; near-equal compute-optimal exponent a ≈ 0.5.
rows.value: Jet-fit exponents and optimal-size estimate as stated in measure.
rows.uncertainty: a range 0.17–0.30; exact optimal size is an extrapolation below the smallest grid model (3.6 × 10^5 parameters).
rows.note: The authors say the exact optimum should not be overinterpreted and the allocation favors data substantially more than model size.
rows.check: The exponent a=0.21 is derived from the fitted law, not measured from IsoFLOP minima. The optimum lies below the smallest grid model, and the split departs from both the Kaplan and Chinchilla splits.
